note: Hardware profiles and per-scanner cost classes for the scanner performance panel. A profile declares a machine's CAPABILITY; a scanner declares its COST; the tuning is derived from the two by monitor/perf-tuning.mjs. It is deliberately not a profile-by-scanner matrix: 11 profiles by 43 checks is 473 cells nobody could keep true, and the first one that went stale would be indistinguishable from a deliberate setting. Every number here is a declared default, not a measurement, except where measuredFrom names a commit. Scanners may declare minDepth to override their cost class: cost is what a run costs, depth is what a run is for, and the two come apart (a secret scan is expensive and belongs at triage depth). Profiles carry modelMatch patterns so the CPU model string is asked first; a name match beats an arithmetic one, and where the real machine has more cores or memory than the profile declares, the MEASURED figure is used and the profile supplies only disk class and container availability.

measuredFrom.coresPerJobHigh: As of 2026-08-22, eleven concurrent sweeps on an 18-core, 48 GB machine drove load to 87 with 1 GB free, and per-repo time rose from 2.6 to 30 minutes. As of 2026-08-23, --jobs 8 on the same machine held load at 96-106. Semgrep alone takes ~2 cores per repository at full intensity, which is where coresPerJob = 2.5 at intensity 5 comes from.

nvme.label: NVMe SSD
nvme.note: Scanners are IO-heavy on checkout and extraction; NVMe is the assumed baseline.

sata-ssd.label: SATA SSD
sata-ssd.note: Roughly a quarter fewer parallel repositories before IO becomes the limit.

hdd.label: Spinning disk
hdd.note: Container image extraction and git checkout dominate. Parallelism past 2 makes a mechanical disk slower, not faster.

network.label: Network or external volume
network.note: Treated as a spinning disk: latency, not bandwidth, is the constraint.

auto.label: Auto-detect this machine
auto.note: Reads the running machine and matches the nearest declared profile. Chosen defaults are shown so they can be overridden.

m4-pro.label: Apple M4 Pro
m4-pro.note: 12-core (8 performance + 4 efficiency) at 24 GB is the common configuration; the 14-core/48 GB part is faster but the defaults here hold for both. Containers run under a virtual machine, which costs roughly 2 cores and 4 GB before any scanner starts.

m5-pro.label: Apple M5 Pro
m5-pro.note: Core and memory figures are read from a host whose CPU model string reports "Apple M5 Pro". Containers run under a virtual machine, which costs roughly 2 cores and 4 GB before any scanner starts.

m3-pro.label: Apple M3 Pro
m3-pro.note: 11-core / 18 GB. Memory rather than cores is the binding constraint once the container VM and a local model are both resident.

apple-air.label: Apple silicon laptop, base (M1/M2/M3/M4 Air)
apple-air.note: The floor case for a modern laptop, and passively cooled: sustained multi-core load throttles within minutes, so the depth ceiling matters more here than the job count.

ryzen5-5600x.label: AMD Ryzen 5 5600X / 5600 desktop
ryzen5-5600x.note: 6 cores / 12 threads. Covers the Ryzen 5 5600, 5600X and 5600G; the 5600 XT is a graphics card, not a CPU. Under Windows, containers run through WSL2, which costs about 2 GB before any scanner starts.

ryzen7-desktop.label: AMD Ryzen 7 / Intel i5 desktop, 8-core
ryzen7-desktop.note: The common self-built desktop: 8 cores, 32 GB, NVMe. Comfortably runs every lane including the containerised ones.

core-i7-2026.label: Intel Core Ultra 7, current generation
core-i7-2026.note: Hybrid performance and efficiency cores. Core count overstates capacity here: the efficiency cores are markedly slower on the single-threaded parsing that dominates several lanes, so jobs are derived from performance cores rather than the total.

dgx-spark.label: NVIDIA DGX Spark
dgx-spark.note: 20 Arm cores with 128 GB of unified memory. Memory stops being the constraint entirely, so every lane can run at full depth concurrently and a local model can stay resident beside them. The GPU is not used by any scanner today; it is available to the LLM-assisted remediation path.

dgx-spark-dual.label: NVIDIA DGX Spark, two linked
dgx-spark-dual.note: Two units over the high-speed interconnect. The job count derived here assumes both are scanning the same fleet from one scheduler; commitwork does not yet distribute a sweep across two hosts, so treat this as the ceiling once it does, not as something the current scheduler achieves.

legacy-hdd.label: Older machine on a spinning disk
legacy-hdd.note: 4 cores, 8 GB, mechanical disk, no container runtime. Every containerised lane is unavailable rather than slow, and the panel says so instead of showing them as passing. This profile exists because 'runs on consumer hardware' has to mean something at the bottom of the range, not only at the top.

light.note: Seconds. Text or config parsing, no index built.

medium.note: Under a couple of minutes on a normal repository.

heavy.note: Minutes. Usually a container, a full history walk, or a network fetch.

very-heavy.note: Builds a database or fuzzes a live target. Tens of minutes to hours; this is the class that decides whether a nightly finishes.

depthLadder.label: full
depthLadder.note: the whole git history — the lane as it ran before ladders

sast.note: Semgrep with --pro-intrafile takes about 2 cores per repository and is the single largest contributor to sweep wall-clock.

depthLadder.label: default
depthLadder.note: p/default plus the local taint rules

depthLadder.label: full
depthLadder.note: adds p/security-audit — the lane as it ran before ladders

sast-opengrep.note: As of 2026-08-26, over 5 repositories of a sample corpus against semgrep 1.172.0 on identical packs: 176s total against semgrep's 806s, worst single repository 94s, and 16s where semgrep took 125s. It is the fastest of the SAST engines here. It carries no `standby` flag, like sast-auto in the same `compare` group, so neither is disabled by default. minDepth is pinned at 4 explicitly so the `heavy` class does not enable it a depth earlier than the lane it is compared against.

sast-codeql.note: Builds a database before it can query.

sast-joern.note: MEMORY-HUNGRY, and that is the binding constraint rather than cores: Joern runs on the JVM and builds a whole-program code-property-graph that it must hold resident to query. The very-heavy class declares 6 GB, and the derivation budgets ramGB minus 4, so this lane is disabled by RAM on any profile under 10 GB — legacy-hdd (8 GB, budget 4) refuses it by name at every depth. That is deliberate: an OOM mid-graph leaves a partial CPG and no artifact, which classifies noscan, but it also costs the whole sweep the time it spent getting there.

sast-bearer.note: A single Go binary, no server and no database build, so it is heavy rather than very-heavy — it walks the tree and runs its rules in process. Classed above medium because it resolves and classifies data flows across files rather than matching patterns line by line.

lint-go-golangci.note: Declared medium alongside gosec, which it runs beside on the same modules — but MEASURED ONLY on a two-file fixture (2 issues, seconds), so this is a placeholder that should be re-measured on a large workspace before it is trusted. golangci-lint type-checks the packages it lints, so a cold module graph is the slow case, not the file count. Unlike clippy it does not execute build.rs or proc-macros, so it does not carry that lane's untrusted-execution question; cgo is the only path to a compiler and only for packages that use it.

sast-python-bandit.note: NOT MEASURED on a real corpus repo — declared light because Bandit is a pure AST walk with no compilation and no module-graph resolution (unlike golangci-lint or clippy), verified on a two-file fixture in milliseconds, but that is the same fixture-only caveat golangci-lint's own entry states and should be re-measured on a sample corpus before this class is trusted for a large Python codebase. No untrusted-execution question at all: Bandit never imports or runs the scanned code, only parses it.

lint-python-ruff.note: NOT MEASURED on a real corpus repo — same placeholder caveat as sast-python-bandit. ruff is written for speed (Rust implementation) and, restricted to --select E,F,W,C90, is doing strictly less work than Bandit's full rule set, so light is if anything conservative, but it is still a guess pending real measurement.

sast-ruby-brakeman.note: NOT MEASURED on a real corpus repo — declared medium rather than light because Brakeman builds a call graph across controllers/models/views (data-flow tracing for its taint checks), doing more work than Bandit's pure per-file AST walk; MEASURED ONLY on a two-controller fixture (~1.2s). Re-measure on a sample corpus before this class is trusted for a large Rails app. No untrusted-execution question: Brakeman parses the app, it does not require or run it.

deps-ruby-bundler-audit.note: Reads Gemfile.lock against the cached ruby-advisory-db (git checkout under ~/.local/share/ruby-advisory-db). As of 2026-09-01, on a 2-gem fixture: under 2s with the DB already cloned; the first run on a machine adds a one-time clone of ~1,400 files, about 15s. Same shape as deps-rust-audit.

sast-php-phpcs.note: As of 2026-09-02, on ten public PHP repositories, phpcs 4.x + pheromone/phpcs-security-audit: a small PHP library 130 files 0.39s/65 MB/143 findings; a PHP logging library 227 0.57s/37 MB/308; a mid-sized PHP application 1232 4.14s/62 MB/317; a PHP ORM 1484 2.95s/55 MB/240; a large PHP framework 3053 10.64s/151 MB/2309. LIGHT CONFIRMED on the binding constraint: peak RSS 151 MB against the 256 MB ceiling, and wall time in seconds. Qualification: it is single-threaded (user/wall ~0.92), so it consumes close to a FULL core rather than the 0.25 this class declares — do not plan four concurrent phpcs runs per core. RAM, not cores, is what keeps it light.

mobile-manifest.note: As of 2026-09-02, on a sample corpus: a Flutter plugin repository (109 manifests among 4,171 files) 0.32s, and under /usr/bin/time 0.52s wall / 0.24s CPU / 55 MB peak RSS, 19 results; an Android image library (61 manifests among 2,980 files) 0.34s, 6 results. Comfortably inside light (0.25 cores, 0.25 GB): ~0.5 cores for half a second and RSS at a fifth of the declared ceiling. Pure file parse — a tolerant tag scan over AndroidManifest.xml / Info.plist, no build, no network, no container.

lint-java-pmd.note: As of 2026-09-02, on three Java repositories from a sample corpus, PMD 7.27.0, the shipped four-ruleset command: a mid-sized Java service 754 files -> 8.3s wall / 37.9s user / 3.94 GB peak RSS; a JVM RPC library 1682 -> 24.7s / 99.9s / 7.51 GB; a large Java project 2616 -> 33.5s / 127.4s / 8.60 GB. Consistently ~4 CORES (user/wall 4.0-4.6x) and never below 3.94 GB even on the smallest sample. The `light` class (0.25 cores, 0.25 GB) would under-declare by ~17x and ~16x, an over-schedule on a scheduler that multiplies by concurrency. WALL TIME IS THE MISLEADING NUMBER HERE: 8-34s reads as `light` ("seconds"), while the binding constraint is memory and cores, exactly as sast-joern records for the same reason. CAVEAT on the RAM figure: with no -Xmx the JVM grows toward 25% of physical memory, so peak RSS is partly heap reservation and would be lower on a smaller machine — the CORE figure is demand-driven and is the one to trust. very-heavy carries minDepth 4, so this lane does not run in shallower sweeps, which is the correct outcome for a 4-core 8 GB lane.

deps-reachability.note: Container with the network severed; builds a dependency graph.

deps-gradle-declared.note: Fetches a transitive closure from deps.dev.

cspm-github.note: Network-bound against the GitHub API, not CPU-bound.

sast-elixir-sobelow.note: Sobelow's own analysis is AST-only and fast; the cost is mix loading the project. Declared, not measured.

lint-haskell-hlint.note: Parses source, builds no index, needs no GHC build. minDepth 2 matches deno-lint, the other light linter gated on a language marker. Declared, not measured.

lint-rust-clippy.note: Declared medium, but this class is optimistic and should be measured before it is trusted: the lane type-checks the crate, so a cold cargo build of a large workspace can exceed medium's 900s timeout. `heavy` (2700s) is the honest class if a measurement disagrees. Not containerised, which is itself the open question — see the check's notes on executing build.rs from an untrusted tree.

sast-codeql-cpp.note: Builds a CodeQL database. Extraction is degraded under build-mode none but the cost is unchanged.

sast-codeql-swift.note: Autobuild compiles the tree and needs full Xcode. The heaviest lane in the fleet.

sast-codeql-csharp.note: Builds a CodeQL database. Does not compile the tree, but the buildless extractor runs its own NuGet restore, so wall clock includes a package fetch and the lane needs network — a cold restore on a large solution dominates the run.

format-rust-rustfmt.note: As of 2026-09-18, on veld (222 deviating files, 1,527 hunks): 2.05s wall / 1.87s user. rustfmt parses each file; no compile, no build.rs, no network.

deps-rust-audit.note: Reads Cargo.lock against the cached RustSec advisory DB. As of 2026-08-28, on a 719-dependency Rust workspace: 5.5s with the DB cached; the first run adds a one-time git clone of the advisory DB.

sast-codeql-rust.note: Builds a CodeQL database, buildless (no build.rs / proc-macro execution). As of 2026-08-26, on a 1,091-file Rust workspace: 5m46s database create + 24m24s analyze; the analyze dominates, and the check's timeoutSec (3600) bounds the pair.

sast-auto.note: Same cost as the sast lane it is measured against.

weak-random.note: Pure text walk over source extensions, no index and no network. As of 2026-08-28: 228 ms on a 397-file repository, 156 ms on a repository of about 750 files. Same class as its sibling stub-detect, and for the same reason.

node-hazards.note: As of 2026-09-02, 963 JS/TS/template files in 0.25s wall. A per-line regex pass with no build, no network, no container and no parse — the walk dominates, not the matching. Directory exclusions come from bin/scan-exclusions.mjs so it never descends node_modules. Re-measure on a large corpus before this class is trusted for a very large front-end monorepo, where the file count rather than the per-file cost is what would move it.

sast-cobol-cobolwork.note: As of 2026-09-21, over a public COBOL corpus: 78 files 1.3s, 161 files 1.7s, 1,232 files 15s, 2,838 files 21s, 619 files 44s, and 4,086 files 1,911s for a complete scan, on a 16 GB machine with other work running. Heavy for that tail, not for the typical repository, which is seconds; the check declares timeoutSec 2700 because the runner's 1800s default would kill a complete run of the 4,086-file repository. Time does not follow file count - 2,838 files took 21s and 619 took 44s - and the 4,086-file repository carries 49,705 unresolved COPY statements; whether those are the cost is not established. A run that cobolwork's memory guard stops early finishes faster with partial coverage, so check a fast large run for partial coverage before believing it. No network, no container, no build.

sast-c-cppcheck.note: AST pass over C/C++ sources. No compilation database, no build, no container, no network — measured seconds on a small fixture.

sast-c-flawfinder.note: Lexical scan of C/C++ sources. Cheapest lane of the C set; it reads text and matches function names.

deps-content.note: Reads one package-lock.json and one package.json per locked package; no walk, no network, no build. As of 2026-09-15: 58-84 ms wall over three runs each on a 70-package lockfile and on the 2-package canary — process start dominates.

agent-instructions.note: Per-line regex pass over instruction files only (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, .cursorrules, copilot-instructions, README.md, docs/**/*.md); no build, no network, no parse. As of 2026-09-15: 33 files in 0.28 s wall, 0.14 s user — process start dominates. Directory exclusions come from bin/scan-exclusions.mjs, so node_modules is never walked.

yara-witness.note: yara-x over the walked file list with CW_YARA_THREADS (default 2) threads, plus one in-process webshell-detect pass for the divergence; no network (rules come from the tool store), no container. MEASURED 2026-10-08 at two threads: about 20 s over ~13k files and about 30 s over ~21k files of two WordPress wp-content trees, 34 s over 27k files of ten PHP projects.

tree-integrity.note: One directory walk for *.dist-info/RECORD, a streamed sha256 of every hashed file a RECORD lists and a walk of the directories RECORDs install into; on a web root (CW_TARGET_MODE=webroot) also git ls-tree, an in-process blob hash of every tracked file, git hash-object over the mismatches only, and three ls-files listings. No network, no build, no container, nothing written to the target. MEASURED 2026-10-08 at a 1-minute load of about 17: 0.08 s on commitwork's own tree (repository mode, one RECORD); 0.65 s wall over a 70 MB pip virtualenv (26 RECORDs, 1,569 hashed files verified, 0 findings); 2.4 s wall for git drift over a 2,486-file, 44 MB checkout. Cost grows with the bytes of installed packages and tracked files, not with the file count alone.

log-evidence.note: Streams every log file in the tree line by line in 4 MiB chunks (gzip decompressed whole), nine regex passes per line; no network, no container. Cost is the tree's log volume, not its size: most source repositories hold none and finish at once. MEASURED 2026-10-08: about 50 s over ~13 M log lines (~500 MB) in a WordPress wp-content tree, about 4 s over ~25 MB of logs in another.

webshell-detect.note: One directory walk that reads every file under CW_WEBSHELL_MAX_BYTES (4 MiB) and windows the larger ones; regex passes per file plus bounded base64/hex/deflate/rot13 decoding (depth 4, 64 children); no network, no build, no container. MEASURED 2026-10-08: about 3 s over ~13k files (~250 MB) and about 5 s over ~21k files (~800 MB) of two WordPress wp-content trees, 45 s over 260,490 files (2.5 GB) across 100 cloned repositories — most repositories finish in under a second.

model-artefacts.note: Directory walk plus an opcode pass over pickle-family files, a header-only read of safetensors, and line walks over dataset yaml/json and python; no network, no build, no container. Whole-file reads are capped by CW_MODEL_MAX_BYTES (256 MiB default; over-cap files are declared skippedOversize). As of 2026-09-15: 345-802 ms wall over three runs on a repository with 4 surface files; the walk dominates. Re-measure on a checkpoint-heavy repository before trusting this class there: cost scales with total pickle bytes walked, not file count.

sast-php-psalm.note: As of 2026-09-02, in degraded mode on ten public PHP repositories, the distribution is BIMODAL rather than sized by the repo. Typical: a small PHP library 1.8s, a PHP logging library 1.5s, a PHP HTTP client 1.6s, a PHP social application 2.6s (1,847 files, 4.9s wall / 7.07s user / 262 MB peak RSS under time -l), a PHP dependency manager 3.8s, a PHP ORM 3.7s, a large PHP framework 45s (3,053 files), a very large PHP framework 46s (11,309 files). Outlier: a mid-sized PHP application (1,232 files) did NOT complete in 2700s. Note the shape — a very large PHP framework is 9x larger than a mid-sized PHP application and finished 58x faster — so wall time does not track file count and a per-repo estimate from size will be wrong. medium (1 core, 1 GB) matches the typical case on resources: ~1.4 cores and 262 MB measured. The outlier is not a cost class, it is a timebox: the check carries timeoutSec 2700 and a timed-out run grades NOSCAN: classifyReport over a killed run's report dir (log present, no sarif, no exit file) returns {sev:noscan, summary:"no output (tool absent/failed)"}. FULL mode (a repo shipping vendor/) is unmeasured.

commit-provenance.note: Two git subprocesses, no tree walk, no network. As of 2026-09-15, under load average ~20: `git log -n 200` with identities and bodies is 86 ms, and the scan end to end is under a second in the ordinary case. The cost that is NOT light is signature verification: %G? makes git run the configured verifier once per SIGNED commit (~50 ms each with gpg.format=ssh), so the same 200 commits took 11 s with it. The lane therefore reads %G? only when monitor/private/branch-protection.json lists the repo with requireSigned:true, and a repo that turns that on should expect roughly 50 ms per signed commit within CW_PROVENANCE_DEPTH.

commit-velocity.note: One git subprocess (`git log -n 500 --name-only` with author and date), no tree walk, no network, no signature verification. Same class as commit-provenance's ordinary case: under a second at depth 500. A lane with no cost class is invisible to tuning, which the perf-tuning test enforces.

agent-config.note: Reads at most five JSON files at the target root, the files their include arrays name inside the tree (at most 256, each under CW_AGENT_CONFIG_MAX_BYTES) and .claude/hooks/** and .claude/commands/**; never walks the source tree, no network, no container. As of 2026-09-15, on fixtures/scan-canary: well under one second wall for either tree, dominated by node start-up.

actions-gaps.note: Reads .github/workflows/*.yml at the root only (no recursion — GitHub reads none either), one block-YAML pass per file, no network, no container, no tree walk. As of 2026-09-16: 0.12-0.13 s wall over three runs on a 3-workflow repository and 0.15 s on a 22-workflow repository (41 jobs); node start-up dominates. Files over 1 MiB are declared skipped rather than read.

actions-health.note: Network-bound, not CPU-bound: 2 + CW_ACTIONS_HEALTH_JOB_RUNS (default 10) gh api calls per repository, no tree walk, no container. As of 2026-09-28, on three repositories: a few seconds each, dominated by API round-trips.

sast-codeql-go.note: As of 2026-10-04, on a 1,818-file Go repository: 1,472s wall (24.5 min) end to end, 1.3 MB SARIF, database 2.6 GB before the analyze step removes it. The lane runs CodeQL's go-extractor per module rather than tracing a build, so the cost is extraction plus analyze and no compilation. A one-file seed is 36s, which is node and CodeQL start-up; treat that as the floor and the 24-minute figure as what a real Go repository costs. timeoutSec 5400 leaves headroom over the measured run. COVERAGE IS NOT THE SAME AS COST HERE: that same run extracted 1,441 of 1,818 files by CodeQL's own count (79%), so a clean result from this lane is partial until the shortfall is explained.

wp-integrity.note: A bounded directory walk to find WordPress installs, one checksum request for core and one per wordpress.org plugin (pool of 4, cached privately; checksums for a published version are reused indefinitely), then md5/sha256 of every file core and each verified plugin ship plus a walk of their directories; no container. Gated on .php sources. As of 2026-10-08: 4.5 s cold (14 requests) and 1.9 s warm over a wp-content backup of ~4.5k plugin files; 5.3 s warm over another of ~5.7k; 3.1 s cold over a complete WordPress release (3,349 files, 2 requests); 2.2 s over this repository.

wp-advisories.note: Reads plugin and theme headers, then one advisory request per distinct plugin and theme slug and one for the core version, plus api.wordpress.org's release list when core is present (pool of 4, cached privately for CW_WPVULN_TTL_HOURS); no hashing, no container. Gated on .php sources. As of 2026-10-08: 3.1 s cold for 18 lookups over a wp-content backup, 1.3 s with most answers cached, 1.4 s over a complete WordPress release, 0.7 s over this repository.

depthLevels.label: Triage
depthLevels.description: Secrets, obvious misconfiguration and hygiene only. Seconds per repository. Answers 'is anything on fire', not 'is this safe'.

depthLevels.label: Standard
depthLevels.description: Adds dependency advisories and workflow auditing. The level most repositories want on every commit.

depthLevels.label: Full
depthLevels.description: Adds container-based supply-chain analysis and full history. The default, and what a nightly sweep should run.

depthLevels.label: Deep
depthLevels.description: Adds data-flow analysis, which builds a database per language. Minutes to hours per repository.

depthLevels.label: Exhaustive
depthLevels.description: Everything, including runtime lanes against a live target and property-based API fuzzing. Intended for a release gate, not a loop.

intensityLevels.label: Background
intensityLevels.description: One repository at a time, reduced rule sets. Leaves the machine usable for other work.

intensityLevels.label: Light
intensityLevels.description: Conservative parallelism. Safe on a passively cooled laptop.

intensityLevels.label: Balanced
intensityLevels.description: The default. Parallelism derived from cores and disk, holding roughly half the machine in reserve.

intensityLevels.label: Committed
intensityLevels.description: Most of the machine. Expect other work to be slow while a sweep runs.

intensityLevels.label: Saturate
intensityLevels.description: Full rule sets and maximum parallelism. On a shared or thermally limited machine this is usually SLOWER end to end than level 4, because contention costs more than the extra parallelism buys. As of 2026-08-22, eleven concurrent sweeps on an 18-core machine took per-repository time from 2.6 to 30 minutes.

comment-schema.what: Slop Bucket: comment blocks over the schema limit, each with a drafted shorter replacement.
comment-schema.runs: on demand from the panel (/comments/, POST /api/comments/sweep); never in a sweep

races.what: Concurrency-bug pass: semgrep race rules, CodeQL concurrency queries, SpotBugs, Infer and ESLint.

build-health.what: Toolchain, format, lint and dead-code health against the tools each repository declares for itself.
build-health.runs: as its own manifest (manifests/build-health.json) for projects that list it

secret-verify.what: Re-checks trufflehog and gitleaks hits against the provider to mark each one verified or not.
secret-verify.runs: after the secrets lanes, on their findings

app-vuln.what: CVEs in applications installed on this machine: a syft SBOM of each app, matched by grype.

scan-images.what: Container images scanned for CVEs with trivy image.

workflow-harden.what: zizmor --fix=safe over GitHub workflows: a remediation that edits files, not a scan.

stpa-sweep.what: STPA re-derivation of the panel and remediation control loop from current code.

bola-sweep.what: Fleet-wide BOLA probe across declared live targets; the per-repo lane is dast-authz-bola.

host-posture.what: This machine: host baseline, egress baseline, config integrity and disk encryption.

package-inventory.what: Installed scanner and package versions against their upstream releases.
